projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with James W. Anderson was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran, James W. Anderson. Mr. Anderson served in the U.S. Army with the 78th Division, 309th Infantry Regiment, First Battalion, Headquarters Company. He served in the European Theater and his highest rank was sergeant. I'm Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mr. Anderson's home at Medina, Ohio, on March 12th, 2004. James was 80 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: In 1941, I was living in North Dakota. Allendale, North Dakota.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you in '41?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: In '41, I was 19.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were out of school at that point?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: No. Actually, I don't. I'm too far down the road age-wise to remember all that, and to try and think back where I was on December 7th is -- I just can't bring it up.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Just don't remember?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: I know that I was devastated. The whole country was. I mean, I was dumfounded that anybody could attack us. Actually, at that time in history, I think we all in America felt as safe as anybody could feel in the face of the earth. Who in the world could even get close to us? Europe was over there. The East was over there. We just didn't have any idea something like that could happen and that's a complete surprise to me. So remembering it --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Is that particular day -- right -- when America went to war did you have thoughts of running out and signing up?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: No. I had a job with the North Dakota Highway Department. I was riding out on a survey team. We were building roads and, of course, we would take the original survey of the land and then we would take the final survey. So I was involved in an operation that was absolutely fantastic, as far as I was concerned, earning $85 a month. And then we started on Highway, 10 which was the one that's through highway -- through North Dakota and Bismarck and Jamestown, and it was a 20 mile stretch that we worked in. And the resident engineer elevated me to office man. I interpolated the movement of earth, and so on and so forth, from the drawings that were made and having a great time. And during that period of time I -- our job finished in this particular area. And I went up across the Missouri to another town, and I didn't particularly care for the reception I had. So I got on the next bus and went home, and that happened in December. Well, December, yeah -- went home and figured I'd go face some college. But as it was, I got greetings from the President, and in March of 1943 I was -- about 12 of us from Allendale went down to Fort Snelling in Minneapolis and was inducted into the Army. So my Army career started in March of 1943.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you joined the Army, was it a tough adjustment to be there with guys from all over the country?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Absolutely not, it was unbelievable. You know, the guys from all over the country are just like you. There's -- same thing -- they -- everybody speaks English. Now, you're in the Army one day and your bunk-mate is your buddy. Just like that, I'd joined. I went in and specifically said that I wanted to go into the Engineers. So as it was, all of it -- I was at Fort Snelling for about two weeks until they got a contingency of guys to go to Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri. My experience -- first experience in the Army weren't the best, because with the name Anderson, KP came up quite often. And I think at Fort Snelling, out of the 14 days I was there, I think I was on KP 11 of them. So I don't know why that -- they must of had a lot of guys -- were not a lot of guys with any name beyond Anderson, or something, or A. And then, when I first got to Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri -- 6:30 in the morning, they let me throw my bag about where I would go to sleep, and then I went on KP until 2:00 o'clock in the morning. I didn't even draw a mattress. So I had a hell of a start at Fort Leonard Wood. At Fort Leonard Wood, they said they came from the plains of Dakota to the Ozark Mountains -- wasn't a great change for me, to say the least. It was devastating change, and I wasn't too happy about trying to dig a fox hole in a bunch of rocks. And so, whenever anything came up to sign up for anything, I signed up for it because I said -- I heard that 6:30 train whistle every morning and I said, "I'm going to be on that train, out of this place." So sure enough, I was selected for the Army Specialized Training Program, ASTP. And from Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri, I was out on that 6:30 train in the morning, listening to that whistle, and saying goodbye Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri. And I was heading out for Laramie, Wyoming, where I went to the University of Wyoming for more testing. After the testing was over, I was on a train heading for Yale University in New Haven, Connecticut. So I spent a year at Yale University in New Haven, Connecticut, from June of '43 to June of '44. Well, you know what happened in June of '44? Okay, D-Day. They closed down every ASTP program. I think the Navy had the same program, and the Air Force had the same program. They closed them all down. All those guys went to the infantry, almost all of us. And as a result of going into the infantry, I ended up in the 78th Lightning Division, which is this one right here. And we were -- been in a regular division and KP was a different story there. Boy, we -- we just -- we just went in and served the meal, and did a little scrubbing and away we were gone. We didn't even stick around during the day. We could go back to the bunks. So KP was really neat. But we trained and I was -- because I was an engineer in Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri, I was in the -- I was put in the A&P Platoon of Headquarters Company, which is the engineers of the infantry -- of the Battalion. So I was in there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What does "A&P" stand for?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Ammunition and Pioneer. Ammunition and Pioneer. A and P Platoon. Ammunition Pioneer Platoon, which is -- we handled all the ammunition, all the blankets, all the tools. We had tools. We didn't have any kind of abundance of tools, but we had tools in case we needed a certain deal. Any blowing up of anything, like -- we had the stuff to do that; and to -- but our primary was getting food, ammo, and bedding to the troops. Working in the front line, continually. So --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where'd you train with the 78th? Where did you train?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Oh. At Camp Pickett, Virginia.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Camp Pickett?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Yeah, and while I was down there in Camp Pickett, Virginia, one day they took our battalion, loaded us into trucks, and drove us to Philadelphia. Philadelphia was having a motorman's strike. They were going to promote another guy to motorman and the guys didn't like that. They didn't want him to make motorman. So they were going to go on strike. Well, I never did figure this out, but they trucked our whole battalion up there. Put us out, I think, it was Franklin Park, in little pup tents and the summer -- summer wear was suntans. And, of course, Philadelphia wasn't exactly the cleanest place during the War because, man, I mean, every factory in the whole U.S. was in operation. I mean, the soot in the grass -- that was something terrible. We were having a heck of a time staying -- looking decent. But the people treated us like the strike never happened. Everybody -- things settled down and I think we were about a week and a half and they shipped us back down to Camp Pickett, or Camp Pickett. Yeah, Camp Pickett. So that was my -- my big experience was sitting in one of these trucks, going through these towns, and the people standing out there wondering where the heck the Army was going to take care of something. But that was great. That was a great time. And then in October -- in October we went overseas. And then from Fort Kilmer -- Camp Kilmer -- from Camp Kilmer, we were moving out of there. Took us in the dark of night, across the bay, loaded on to the ship called the John S. Ericsson and it's 2:00 in the morning. And we got up the next day, and we're still in the dock and all of New York is driving by and everything else. And we're going "What, what the dickens did they take us across the bay at 12:00 o'clock at night in the dark?" And figuring that was a secret operation, they was going to have us out on the ocean by morning, and here we are still docked. So it was kind of a surprise to all of us guys that we were there. Well anyway, we were in a convoy coming across. Quite a number of ships and, I reckon, there were destroyers on both sides to protect us, because we went across without incident and landed in Southampton, England. And from Southampton, England, we went by train down to Bornemouth, England, and there we were billeted for a couple -- three weeks, and then we got on a -- on a English ship. Did you ever smell mutton cooking? But anyway, that smell was enough to keep you on the rails, away from the kitchen. But that's what they fed us. We landed, I reckon, we landed in Le Havre. But I don't know if that was where it was. And during the night, a pretty good wind came up and we started bouncing against another ship in the harbor, and we said, "Boy, this is something else." But I guess, at that time, they must've used everything for -- for transporting. Because, oh man, there were guys -- there was just -- just a tremendous amount of troops that were used by the Service. They took us to a field. Well, trucked us to a field. Let's see, was it there? It was there they put us on a boat. They gave us the candy bar that you eat one a day. You have a third of it as breakfast, a third of it at lunch, and a third of it at dinner time. Well -- so we were given that. We were billeted in a farmer's field and was in a hill, like this. And I was down here in the valley and it started to rain and I -- all these hundreds of guys that were billeted there -- walking on that land. It started to -- everything started to slow down there. So I was building up a dike and had to keep mud out of my pup tent -- well, two of us, so we wouldn't smother to death if the damn thing came. But, oh, it was horrible. Then they served us at Thanksgiving time, and they served us Thanksgiving dinner -- brought that out, turkey. But by the time I got my pan -- my mess kit -- got it filled up with the goodies and walked back to my tent, I had a mess kit full of water. Needless to say, it wasn't the most delicious meal. But at least it was a turkey, and at least it was something to eat besides a candy bar -- one of those. So we enjoyed -- that was nice. And from there -- we weren't there but three days, I guess -- four days. And then they loaded us on the railroad, forty and eight. Do you know forty and eight? Okay. We went from forty and eight from Le Havre, France to a place, I think it was Verviers, Belgium. But I don't know that. I mean -- well, when you were in the Army, you don't know where you are, and nobody tells you either. But anyway, we billeted there. And the first night we were there, about 9:00 in the evening, there was a roar overhead, and we looked up. And what the heck is that? Going over us was one of those V-2's that Hitler was throwing, and then the motor cut out when it was over us and we figured, uh oh. So it was aimed for some place, might of been aimed at us, I don't know, but they missed us by a few miles because it was on down the road in some part of -- well, Belgium and Holland come together. Holland comes down a little bit into Belgium, so we were in that area. And we were there just until December 13th. And December 13th, we went into combat and we hit the Siegfried Line. Now, the reason I knew that was because I knew a little bit of history. And we were going down this road, and I look over there and, by golly, there's a pillbox. And I said, "Well, for crying out loud." I hadn't seen any dragon's teeth, but there's the pillbox and I said, "Jeepers-Christ, we've got to be on the Siegfried Line." So and they -- company there we had an anti-tank outfitted with a 57 cannon on the wheels. And Old Nick, we said -- this guy said, "Let's get Nick." Now get this, we don't know where we are, we don't know who we're fighting, or where they are. We're just going down the road. So we get Nick and his 57, and we said, "Nick, do you see that thing right over there? That round thing?" "Yeah." "See those slits in it?" "Yeah." "Well, that's a pillbox." "See, if you can put a 57 right through one of those slits." Boy, he crank that thing up. Well, we weren't from here to that building over there away from it, a bit more maybe. Boy, that 57 shell must of just raised Cain in there. It must of, because about six guys came out from -- bleeding from those concussion, and it must of been horrendous. And I don't know why they didn't fire at us, maybe they had fired at us and fired everything they had. It was -- it was a situation -- it was really crazy and that was my -- and so, what we hit on that first day in combat, was the northern end of the German build-up for the Battle of the Bulge. And as we found out later, the Corp, the German Corp that was up in this area, was to come through Kesternich and turn north, and go up towards the North Sea. Well, we were a division in the -- where they went -- where they broke through with the 102nd, I believe it was strung out over about a 20 mile stretch, and that's where they went through. Well, we were a whole division in less than a mile of area. So we took a wicked beating there. That was my first day under-fire.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember what you were feeling in that first day in combat?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Well, we ended up in a farm house in this town of Simmerath and, of course, the basement was the place to be. And then we had to post guards, and they had black wall of stone, about this high, around this front area of this house. Well, that's where we posted ourselves because we were getting artillery raided, and I mean to tell you, they was throwing stuff in there. All over the place. We lost our lieutenant and our platoon sergeant that first night, through artillery fire. But gosh, I was out there on duty -- guard duty. And man, I never heard so doggone much stuff fly over. And a lot of it landed and never exploded. And then there were some that exploded. And it seemed to be about -- maybe 300 yards beyond us. But I'm sure they must of been firing at us, because Kesternich was a roadhead where they were going -- where the Germans were going to use for their transportation and stuff like that. And, of course, we hit this town -- the 311th. I was in the 309th, and the 311th came in and hit this area, and the house-to-house fighting over in that area. And we stopped the Germans right there. We stopped them cold, but we took a hell of a beating. And so in this process of everything happening to us, first time out, we lost a lot of guys in the 309th. So about ten days after the fight, after the -- we went into combat. They pulled us off line, off of our battalion and we went back to Aachen. And our unit was assigned to guard the ammunition dump. Oh man, talk about a dump. Jeepers-criminy, talk about the ammunition dump. In this Battle of the Bulge picture that they show, they go for that ammunition dump. Well, that was like this dump. I said, "Jeepers-criminy." So when I see that picture, when they show the Battle of the Bulge, I think "Goll-darn it. I wonder if that was the ammunition dump they were thinking of taking." Because while we were there the skies broke, and the planes could come out, and there's some P-38's. A squadron of four or five flying over us. Boy, we looked up and they were getting ready to peel off and -- hey, hey -- they think this is a German dump. Old (?)Mickelack climbs up on the truck with the old 50-caliber, and he's going to take them on. And anyway, we had ribbons of collars that you put across the top of the truck for identification. And I said "Boy, we get those out right now." And we did. We got them on the truck so that they took off, but Mike had his -- had his 50-caliber up there firing at them. So anyway, we had that. So and then, at that time, (?)Burnell had moved up to platoon sergeant. And he came to me and took me down the road, and asked me if I'd wanted to be sergeant of the Third Squad. I said, "Sure. I'll be sergeant of the Third Squad. So I was promoted on Christmas Day in 1944. So I was in charge of the Third Squad, and the Battle of the Bulge culminated right in there. They got tanks. We held our end. We held the northern tier, and then the Battle of the Bulge closed down. I don't know why we never closed the gap north and south, and got them all in there. I don't ever know why that -- all we did was push them back. But we ended up in the Hurtgen Forest and the Hurtgen Forest was probably the boondoggle of all places to put anybody, because the Germans had quadranted that off, so that they could place a doggone shell anywhere they wanted to, and tree bursts. Thirty-thousand American troops were wounded or killed in that damn Hurtgen Forest. Well, good thing we didn't know -- we didn't know about that, then. But we had the guys that had been there -- had very industriously -- had built or taken about three logs and put them up, and dug out a hole, and then covered them with logs. And we had a little hut that would hold six guys sleeping side-by-side. And we had a cover, and also, we had a stove. The tin cans they we got from the -- and we put a can of gas and lit it, and we had a chimney going up; and very did serve the purpose, but looked pretty antique, colonial. We had set up a whole perimeter of traps and, well, exploding -- and forgot what the names of all those things were.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Grenades and mines?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: No. We didn't set up mines. We only set up -- just a trap of -- if anybody came along and tripped it, we knew someone was over in the area. So -- but about that time, we were right close to a fire break in this Hurtgen Forest. And about that time, I think, the Germans had figured that there ain't much left to this war, so they didn't. They fired into us every night. At about 6:00 o'clock they would fire in, and all the shells would land in the firebreak. They never came any further than that into -- where we were. And our cooks came up one time, about the firing time, and set up their stuff. And they started throwing their stuff in and, boy, those cooks took off and left all of their -- us guys had to go there and feed ourselves. There was nobody there to dish it up. But yeah, it wasn't a pleasant sight. But when you been in it then, it gets old -- stuff. You know? So we just laughed. We went ahead and ate, because we knew all the shells were going to fall anyway. And they did. And then we went into combat, and the Schwammenauel Dam was the dam on the Rhur River. They tried to bomb it and everything. They -- they could never get to it. I don't know why. Then I saw a story on that -- on a show one time. They tried to invent a torpedo, or something that they could drop from the air and get it in there to blow up some of these dams. They didn't have a lot of success with it, or something. The torpedo pop up -- whatever it was, it just couldn't. Well anyway, the dam is still standing and it's on the Rhur River. And if the Germans had blown it, it would -- would've flooded everything, from this area north -- to the North Sea. And anything on the east side of the river would have been trapped, because there would have been no way to get over there. Well, they had to build dams or bridges of some kind, until the water went down. So everything was held up on the west side of the Rhur River until this dam was secure. And our outfit -- my battalion secured the dam. And then the squad, my squad and I, had the honor of going down and inspecting the dam for charges, and so on and so forth. And, of course, following orders and away we go, and without a lot of incidents or anything else we got down and checked it out. And we didn't trip any wires and blow up the dam. But I guess it's -- your expendable. So I figured that being the case, why -- looked like everything was all right. So, of course, the engineers got in on it, too, so they were down there. And, well, the dam was secured and then -- and then we finally started moving out. And we went cross the Rhur River, down -- up-stream and -- well, down-stream I guess, would be toward the North Sea -- the town of(?)Blintz and in the town of Blintz -- had been completely flattened. There wasn't a thing standing in Blintz, except a statue in the center of town. And wouldn't you know, it -- the statue stood, had an arm up, like this. The telephone lines that the guys laid would run up to that statue. Then these guys would climb the statue, and throw the line over this guy's arm. So this telephone line came up and over his arm. I said, "You can't believe the American guy, he got a sense of humor, no matter where he's standing." Well anyway, that was something. The only thing standing in that town and -- (Brief interruption) -- and then we went across this -- well -- the Schmidt, Germany. When we got there, the Keystone Division of Pennsylvania had tried to come through that area to get to Schmidt, and to get to Schwammenauel Dam. Well, in the dam -- and, man, they'd been mowed down by -- because the build-up was there. And in November -- and out of this field laid, I know, just a whole bunch of American guys that had been slaughtered in the fight. And the order come down that those -- those veterans are to be picked up immediately. Now listen, they laid there from November until the end of January in that cold weather, and they was froze solid, of course. Well, you know who got the job? Third squad got the job, right? I'd never seen so many boots in my life, because I tell you it was just terrible. Not only that, but how we had to treat them. There's only one way to get them out of there, and that was to pile them like cord wood on the trucks. And then took them to the aid station, and that's where we cut them off like cord wood again. And I just, just didn't -- wasn't something I needed at that time. It was something. You get orders. You do it. So I did it, but I didn't like it. That wasn't my job. That wasn't my MO, but anything happens in war, right? So that was a very,very sad thing I saw -- was that it makes you wonder, you know, right then and there, what the hell it's all about. And then we went across the Cologne Plain. And we're out in the plain there, and we were bogged down because of the traffic. It was so fast moving and we were -- we were in an area where -- wide-open to any observation. And our guys were standing in a circle around the trucks. Of course, we had our stuff. Our ammunition and food and all that stuff. And, by-golly, if a shell didn't land right next to us. And we had a -- I think six of the guys were hit there. And, oh boy, my squad was hit pretty bad. And I happen to be in the truck waiting for clearance and I hopped out of the truck. And gosh, there's Bernard and he's pretty well shot up. Shot up, blown up by that damn piece of shell. And I think I used a couple of bandages. We had packs of bandages each one of us carried. I used a couple of them, trying to bandage him up to stop the bleeding. And right in the middle of all this -- and, dog-gone, if medics didn't show up with a jeep, and they immediately took him, and put him on a stretcher, and got him on that jeep. And so, I figured then -- I didn't know until after I got this book that he died. He was dead. Maybe I was treating a dead guy, I don't know, but that was one part I didn't particularly care for. We went on there, and we went on to Ahr, Germany -- Ahrweiler,Germany, which is on the Ahr River. And the Ahr River flows into the Rhine, just above Remagen. Well, just about the time we're securing this area, dog-gone it, they aren't attacking the bridge. So the next morning, where were we? We were on our way to the bridge and, oh, I guess, we cleared the bridge at about 10:00 o'clock in the morning. And when they started the Battle of the Bulge, the Germans used german guys dressed up in American uniforms, you know. So when we got on the other side, I got instructions that I was to stand down there on the river's side, and stand all of our units north to (?)Hanau. And so, I had figured that I was a long, lanky, skinny -- they called me "Pencil with Ears" in those days -- guy -- that they figured I would of been enough of a noticeable piece in the whole works, so they'd all know who that guy was. Well, as it was, there was a another long, lanky string bean from the 9th Division that was stuck in the same place. And what we were in an over -- in an underpass. Under a railroad, right at the river's edge. It was just about -- it was a little roadway, way out there, but then we were right at the river. But they must use this to get up to that tunnel. They'd come and get under the railroad and get up there. So we stood in there, and his -- his outfit was scheduled for Hanau, and they wanted him to send his outfit to Linz. What they were doing was changing our two units. We were both to go to Linz, but instead we would go to Hanau. So, of course, I stood there, and anything that came through, that I'd saw the numbers on the bumper, or something like that. Well, I -- and needless to say, a Captain might -- would give me a hard time, "Sergeant, what is this?" "Sir, I've been instructed to send all of our -- all of our units north, to Hanau." And he was sitting there. He had his feet up on the dashboard of the jeep, smoking a cigar. Man-oh-man, that's a good bit of comfort in this situation. But anyway, he finally didn't give me any more guff. He got out there, and away he went up to Hanau. So, at least, I got him convinced. Yeah, I spent the whole day there directing this traffic that was coming across. If there was any of my units -- there, I was. So was the other guy. So another sequel to that. I came home after the war and went to Allendale. Went back to school. Graduated. Went to teaching. My wife came from out here, also, to Dakota to teach in the same school I was in. And as it so happened, we got married in Barberton. And her friend -- her best friend, Donna, married Don Swinehard. And we were playing cards with them one day, after we were married, and you know what? "What did you do in the war, Don?" "Well, I was in the 9th Infantry." "You were?" "Yeah." Well, we compared places where we'd been. He was the guy that was standing in that goll-damn place, directing with the 9th to the -- Linz, and that was the guy. And I said, "This is unbelievable. How could that happen? You're from Orrville, Ohio, and me from Allendale, North Dakota." Two girls know each other, you don't see things like that happening too much. It was crazy. But anyway, he was the guy that was standing underneath there. We talked about the anti-aircraft piece of equipment that got hit, and we got knocked on our butts by something that landed in that hill. Boy, what a blast and a dead hiney [sic] laying right there, and all this stuff. And we compared it, and I said, "Hell, he was the guy." Then we went from there. Of course, the 78th was the first full infantry unit across the Rhine River, in the heartland of Germany. We got everybody across. Matter-of-fact, part of our 78th was with the 9th Armored, the infantry -- the 310th. Some guys went with and captured that bridge. They don't say that much. They give all the credit to the 9th Armor, but the 78th Division was right there. We were the first full infantry division across the Rhine, into that pocket. So we went from there, up north, went across the Seine River, went into the lower part of the industrial heart of Germany, which was Dortmund, Wuppertal and Essen, just across the river from Cologne. That was -- that was the manufacturing center. And, of course, the war was winding really down then. And, oh, I guess our division took thousands of prisoners, just thousands of them. But we didn't guard them or anything. We just -- they were in units of four coming down the road and just going, streaming into these -- into our compound. I guess the need for a little bit of food didn't discourage them. Knowing that and figuring that they'd get fed. And they got fed, they did. As best they could. So that was the end of the war for me, as far as shooting. I was strafed. I was bombed. I was artilleried and I was shot at. And I'm here in one piece, and I'm thankful for that. There was a lot of guys who didn't. I didn't see a lot of it. I didn't put any notches on my gun, because you can't. How do you know, you know? So you were shooting. So what did you hit? So anyway, then we were billeted in a little town of (?)Helmichshausen, and while we were in Helmichshausen, Nick, the guy that had the -- was from Missouri, we did a little poaching. Old Nick figured out, you put the light on the jeep, and we'd go out at 9-10:00 o'clock at night, and we'd get a -- some food for the compound. And so, we did. And so --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Is that a deer or an elk?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's a deer?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's got a real good rack on it.

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: 11-point buck.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Nick was an Arkansas boy, lived in the back country of Arkansas. And they -- I guess they eat food like this. You know, it's whatever is available to them in their heartland. And flooding of the Missouri -- Mississippi River left big catfish in ponds. So he could skin a deer and, you know, take care of --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: So yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Good looking trophy piece, too.

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Yeah. There's a picture of Schmidt, Germany, the town that the Schwammenauel Dam was on. And you could see that the houses were in very fine shape. You had to use a blanket to keep the sun out, and put it on the doors. So, pretty well beat up.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any close buddies in your outfit?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Not necessarily. I had one guy, (?)Vanderhoff, from Wisconsin. And there's a guy by the name of Milton (?)Sandeford. He's still alive in Atlanta, Georgia, but I didn't buddy with him. And this Dominic Mastrianni was probably my closest little buddy. As a sergeant, you don't need buddies, and I tried not to get too close. As far as buddies go, no, I would say I didn't -- Nebraska -- or (?)Brunell lived in Stowe, and I saw him, before he died, several times. I didn't know they lived this close. See, I thought he was in Pennsylvania, boy, but a North Dakota boy? If there's another one in the unit somewhere, you're lucky. There ain't that many. I was in with New Yorkers, Pennsylvanians. That was primarily -- primarily the group that was in there. But in that 78th, what the heck? A bunch of guys from New York? In a little town of Allendale, our weekly paper -- and the weekly paper consists of Mrs. Jones, who has York Township, would listen on the phone and write down -- and so, it would be in the paper. Well, these New York guys, they just loved that paper because if it came in, they'd grab it from the mail guy before it got to me. And then they'd open it up, and they would sit there and read these, and they'd just howl. Just howl. They thought that's the craziest thing they ever saw; Mr. and Mrs. So and So visiting -- but that's big news out there, you know? For everybody. But they thought that was really something. So they got a kick out of my Allendale Reader.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have other memories of mail call, getting packages, or whatever?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: I'll tell you one mail call. There was a boy from South Dakota in Communications and his name was Robert G. Anderson. Well, I have a brother named Robert F. Anderson. And my mother wrote a letter one day to me, but she wrote Robert F. Anderson -- and my address, and my brother was in the Merchant Marine. So when it came to my post, the guy at my place, he put down KIA in it and sent it back. But he knew damn well that I -- where it came from and I was the only guy in the outfit from North Dakota. And why in the hell he sent that back, but the minute by mother got the letter, she saw what she had done. She had put my brother's name and my address, and so she wasn't concerned about it -- that. But, boy, that was a hell of a thing. To get a letter like that back, you know, KIA. Well, mail call wasn't that great. I think probably one of the worst things about it, was we went 128 days without a shower. Never saw one. Never saw a shower in 128 days. That's what they say in the book, was a 128 days. I think it was longer than that because I took a shower in Belgium, when we were in that field up there, just before we went into battle. And I never, ever saw another shower until we got to Wuppertal, Germany. And I don't even remember if there was a shower there. But anyway, it was a long time between. I think they figured that if you get bumped off, you won't smell so bad anyway. So what the hell? That's a bit of humor. But in -- in the process of having been in Helmichshausen, our outfit was chosen for Berlin occupation. So sure as hell, we went across the little strip of land there, that the Russians owned. Through the check-point, and we had to get into the American sector of Berlin. And I walked the street with the Russians and smoked cigarettes with them, graced the path, because we'd take over the old boy, and taken and made his life miserable. And that was my experience there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any encounters with German civilians there?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: No, we -- the girls? They were -- the Russians were brutal with them. Americans have a different way of approaching things. This was great about the American guys. This was -- most of them, they're not brutal. Russians rape, pillage, and all that crap. And we just didn't do that stuff. I was proud of them. Proud of our guys because we had a lot of experiences. We were -- I think there were four or five of us, were with these five German girls in Berlin, and fraternization was a no-no, but pfffffft on that. The girls were -- and what they did, they got cigarettes or anything colorful, and they'd sell them to the Russians. And then they say (spoke Russian). "Nice deal, nice deal." But we went into this building. They lived upstairs in this building. And I'm looking at the building and there ain't another building for blocks. It's the only building standing, and it was not a very big one. And I'm thinking, "Jeepers-criminy, I don't know." So I went upstairs with them, anyway. But I told some of the guys, I said, "Look I'm not comfortable here. If you guys started having fun with those girls, rocking the boat, this whole damn building is going to collapse because it's gotta be sitting on its last timber." Somewhere after -- with all the devastation I saw around it, but I was amazed. This one building, it's only a two-story building. I don't know what other kinds of buildings were around, but America and the British and the Russians just devastated that city. Just devastated it. And the Brandenburg Gate was the only thing standing in the -- on any account, I can't understand a guy subjecting a country to something like that. I guess it's a dictator, they don't give a damn. Like Saddam, they don't care. Leave it a hole in the ground, if you have to. He did. So the experience in Berlin was super. I can't knock it. I was sorry that after I'd left, and after several years, you know, with the Wall, you know -- said we're going to keep this, just as it is. And they did. Boy, I guess they didn't do anything much there, really. So that was the -- it was the end of my career in the Army because in -- right at the end of '44, they shipped us. Well, you had a point system and, you know, and I believe I had 65 points. So I was -- all the guys that wanted to, with 65 points, could go home. So I chose to get the heck out of there. And I did. And I went to Bremerhaven. And while we were in Berlin, we stood reveille and retreat, and all we -- I mean, we were -- we were spick-and-span as far as conducting ourselves in front of the Germans. But when I got to Bremerhaven, it was eat when you want to eat, and eat what you want to eat. What? No reveille, no retreat, that's right. You're going home. You're -- boy, that was a treat. Then we loaded the boat, and I got on the boat. And you know what boat I got on? The S.S. John Ericsson same damn boat I went over on. And that doesn't happen very often. And I landed in New York. We were in the North Atlantic storm so bad, that the boat, as huge as it was, went down into a swell, like this, and you could look up at the top, like this, up at the next swell. My bunk was in the rear-end of the ship and when that ship came up on top of that swell, you could hear the old propeller clunking out in the air. Clunk, clunk, clunk, clunk, clunk. Well, all of a sudden, it stop because it went back down into the valley again. Goll-Friday, we spent 14 days, or something like that, going -- if the purser plotted it on the -- we'd go down, take a look at it, see where we'd been that day, because it looked like we went back to Europe there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: "Forced" is the exact --

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Had to stay into the wind, I guess. But that was a heck of a trip home. Then when we pulled into the harbor. We had 5,000 guys on the ship, 4,999 of them were on the starboard side looking at the Statue of Liberty. And I was up on the -- on this side, because I figured if that -- damn, if that captain kept saying, "Some of you guys move over, because you got me almost at 45 degrees. And another degree or two, and we're going to capsize." So I said, "Well, Anderson, I tell you what. If we're going to capsize." So I crawled up the deck plate and got to the other side. I figured it would throw me. That was crazy. But we did make it into port. He finally -- if he'd straighten the ship out, so he was pointed right at the Statue of Liberty, he'd been a lot better shape. But going sideways to it? But anyway, we got there. And then I got home. I was at Camp McCoy, Wisconsin and I was discharged there. And you know who the people were who took my equipment? Germans.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Captured? Prisoners?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Enjoying it. Loving it. And I know that dang-well -- a lot of them didn't go home. They had it. Man, they couldn't believe it. They couldn't believe that they could be treated that well, and fed and clothed, and not going back to that crap over there. I don't blame them. And then I got on the train and came home to Allendale. Finished out my college career and went to teaching.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you finally got home?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Well, my brother was dating a girl, and he didn't bother to see me until a little later on. And my sister was just a kid in high school, and she had friends that she was out gallivanting with. And my mom and dad warmly welcomed me home. So it wasn't any kind of a great big joyous -- as matter of fact, I think I had to hitchhike from Aberdeen to Allendale, I think. I don't know how I got up there -- they -- how could I contact them? You had to use the phones and -- but I knew how to do it. So I hitchhiked before, so I didn't -- didn't mean anything to me. And anybody who saw a soldier, you could -- just about anybody would pick you up in those days. Didn't have any problem at all. So I'm sure I made it up to Allendale in record time. Forty miles, but I think that's how -- I can't even remember that, you know, and I can't remember what -- where I slept and where I slept in Berlin. I can't remember that and I go, goll-darn it. How can I -- how can it be so dumb to not be able to. A buddy of mine who lived right here in Allendale, Robert McMillan -- the USO -- I signed my name in on North Dakota. He signed his name right under mine. He was with the 69th and they disbanded that, and some of the guys went to the 78th. So he ended up going into the 78th on duty in Berlin, and he signed his name right under mine, and we still get together. He lives in Stowe.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that a USO in Berlin?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what kind of entertainment did you get there, at the USO?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Tell you what, I probably was in a situation that never really got a known star, or anybody while I was there. I never saw a star, or movie star, anywhere. Of course, now, when we went into combat in December, we were never, ever relieved by another unit so that we were taken back to a shower area or anything. The only relief we had, when we were relieved, we were on duty at that ammo depot and we weren't overly crowded with guys -- so kept a lot of those guys and eventually, man, we started off. I think we had ten guys to a squad. Thirty-some guys made up the platoon and, man, we were down to five guys a squad there. They never replaced anybody. It just doubled up the work for everybody. Whatever we had to do -- it was crazy. Just wasn't a lot of replacements for -- so from December 13th until the landing in Wuppertal, Germany, I don't think we had a couple of days just as a rest -- at the Seine River, but that was just to get the bridges and everything going. We never -- like I said, we never saw a shower in 128 days. So we were always on duty combat, and that's the way it went. This is why I can't understand why they put a girl out there, under those conditions. Goll-damn it, if I can't understand a girl wanting to live under those conditions. I know that Iraq deal has got to be murder. It's gotta be murder. We -- we used a slip, I don't know how many. Six months? I used a slip trench. Girls use a slip trench? Jeepers-crap, that's something else. So I don't understand that -- that girls in the military, particularly in the infantry, it makes sense.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: It makes sense.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think of your experiences during World War II, does any other particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Going over on the Ericsson, my buddy and I, who was a buddy from -- from Yale, he ended up in the Engineers. We sat in the prow of the boat, right up in the prow and looked out over the land, and looked out over the ocean. And that was a fun time, because the ocean was as smooth as it could be. It was just beautiful. Couldn't do that coming back, but going over was nice. No, I haven't. Nothing other than what I told you. That really was -- we ran into situations that were all I had. One, yeah, I had one. I know one. We were assigned to the C Company, and we were going to work with the Engineers on sealing the Autobahn. We were the first outfit to seal the Autobahn on the east side of the Rhine, and we were with C Company. C Company was decimated. I don't think they had 20 guys in this outfit, and I had five. So we were all in reserve, and I was in reserve, waiting to be called up to go up on the front line and get on up there. And, good-gosh, all of a sudden, we looked up to our right and coming down the dog-gone valley was a hundred German soldiers with their hands, like this. And what the hell? And the lieutenant looked at me, and he says, "What am I going to do with that." And I said, "Gosh, I don't know. Can you spare a guy?" But yeah. Well, he'd -- I guess he got two guys to go with him. To take them back to -- to the POW camp but, boy, that was a surprise. I never expected that. Never expected that. And their leaders were right out in front, leading them right down. They were ready to call it quits, and rightly so. Smart move. It was a smart move because we had a lot of -- that first ten days, before that bridge collapsed, there was lot of equipment that went across that bridge. And, oh boy, and engineers kept getting hit by artillery. And I saw -- I saw the first jet plane there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: There. They used that jet plane.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Near Remagen?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: At Remagen. They used that jet plane because we wondered, "What the hell was that?" Because it went zoom. Goll-friday, goll-damn made a run and dropping the bomb. The bomb missed the bridge, good thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Just a single jet though, just one?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Yeah. They had one up, that I know of. If they had more than that -- I think it came over a couple times but, of course, we were busy and we couldn't watch all the action out there, and watch for our guys, and that's a lot of turmoil. A lot of guys moving. A lot of equipment moving because the -- they did a good job. I think, probably, the logistics of something like that has gotta be horrendous. When we get a part of a unit across, it comes under the command of another guy that's crossed him. Another unit, the 310th, was granted by the -- not the armor guy, and stuff like that, until you get it all together. 310th went that way. The 309th went that way. And the 311th went that way. Now, you got to get the 310th with their unit, jeepers-crap, the logistics have gotta be horrible. I didn't worry about that. I didn't know where I was, and I did didn't know where we were going. But, boy, I was there. Yeah. So I saw a lot of action. Tremendous amount of action. I don't think that I've seen as much artillery and anti-aircraft that were at the Remagen Bridge, lining the river, because they had everything they could get together to throw it. Anything coming over that's going to take out that bridge, and those Engineers did a beautiful job. Because I don't know where they got the planks. They got the planks from somewhere. It must've been around in there, available to them because, boy, they kept coming out on that bridge and laying planks down. And shells were getting -- blowing them away and they'd plank it up. And they would get the equipment moving, and the equipment moved steadily across that bridge. It wasn't holed up at all, that I could see when I was there. Now, there were probably other times when they got it worse than that. But right there in the beginning, it was pretty well taken care of. Yep, it sure was. Yep. I wouldn't have wanted to been a guy in a tank, because I saw that in Schmidt, when they made that attack with the Pennsylvania outfit, Keystone Division, looking down this hill, I saw tank, tank, tank, tank. Goll, they were blown right out. Must've stood at the top of the hill with an 88, and just fired right back at them. Bang, bang, bang, bang, bang. Oh, that to me was -- I don't know. So those are things -- but the towns, the devastation. The -- just the ruination just amazed me. The town that we went in the first one, that the house was standing and the barn was standing -- I was up to Kesternich, right there, on the front line, holding out blankets and food, like that. We were there a day and a half, and when I came back, all of that was flat. Just flat. Nothing there anymore, and I'm thinking, "Good gosh, I'm glad I was up at Kesternich." But that was bad. Too bad they don't give you a road map and tell you what's going on. But this thing here. I was going to show you one picture in here. That's the -- that's the platoon I was with. They were on rest-break.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: I don't know if I'm in there or not. If I am, I'm one of the guys laying down. I didn't see the picture being taken. Well, the guys in the front here -- but I recognized the guys.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you guys get to talk over home, mail, girls, previous actions, food, and the future?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Yeah, in that order, I think. Girls came first.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly. They got girls.

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. And I think, right here, this guy here, won the Congressional Medal of Honor at Kesternich. He's the only guy in the division that won it, and we honor him. He's at Keyser, West Virginia, and our division goes up and honors him. We have -- we have a pretty active alumni association, and we go up to Keyser to honor him on his birthday.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Staff Sergeant Jonah E. Kelly, he's buried there?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Yep. He's buried in West Virginia. Yep, and he -- Kesternich, where I was. Yep.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Company E, 311th Infantry.

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Very good.

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: It shows our maps in there, of our -- there's the bridge across the Rhine.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: The guy said -- the engineer said, when the 78th finally got far enough inland to knock out those -- that artillery, we didn't get it anymore.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow. Well, very good. I think that about covers it.

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Pretty much. Pretty much. As far as I was concerned, I was awarded a Bronze Star for Meritorious Service.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that for a specific action?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Meritorious service, not specific.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: For your overall contribution?

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Yep. Yep. So I'm proud of that. At the time I got it, it was five points. That made me happy. It helped that -- to start, but now I've gotten to appreciate the Star.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: So it was a special tribute, right. We were awarded a Presidential Citation for the capture of the Schwammenauel Dam. So yeah, there are a few things that are noteworthy. But outside of that, it was just war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: And this is -- all of this, and I suppose you get it all like this, don't you?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No, they're all different.

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: They're all different?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I hear different things all the time. Well, even the guys that were involved in the same thing. I talked to other guys that were involved in Remagen, and they -- there's a little different things you hear about that all the time.

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You know, it's all part of the big picture.

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. I talked to several guys that were involved in the Remagen thing.

sp.speaker: James W. Anderson
sp.p: It'd be in the 9th Armor. (Tape cut out)
